summary: Jesus answers complaints that He welcomes sinners with three parables of lost things found, ending with an older brother who refuses to join the feast.
key_insight: The complaint was, “This Man receives sinners and eats with them.” Jesus’ final scene answers it: a father outside a feast, pleading with the son who never left home. The story stops before the older brother replies, and the Pharisees listening were left to decide whether they would go in.
story: Tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear Jesus. The Pharisees and scribes complained, “This Man receives sinners and eats with them.” So Jesus told them a parable.

What man with a hundred sheep, if he loses one, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the lost one until he finds it? He lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing, and calls his friends and neighbors: “Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost!” “I say to you that likewise there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine just persons who need no repentance.”

Or what woman with ten silver coins, if she loses one, does not light a lamp, sweep the house and search carefully until she finds it? She too calls her friends and neighbors to rejoice with her. In the same way, “there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”

Then He said, “A certain man had two sons.” The younger asked for his share of the estate, and the father divided his livelihood between them. Soon the younger son gathered everything, went to a far country and wasted it with prodigal living. When a severe famine came, he hired himself out to feed a man’s pigs, and he longed to eat the pods the pigs were eating. No one gave him anything.

When he came to himself, he said, “How many of my father’s hired servants have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!” He would go home and say, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son.” So he set out. But while he was still a great way off, his father saw him and had compassion, and ran and fell on his neck and kissed him. The son began his confession, but the father called for the best robe, a ring, sandals and the fatted calf: “for this my son was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.”

The older son was in the field. Coming near the house, he heard music and dancing, and a servant told him why. He was angry and would not go in, so his father came out and pleaded with him. He answered, “Lo, these many years I have been serving you; I never transgressed your commandment at any time; and yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might make merry with my friends.” Yet as soon as “this son of yours” came home, he said, after devouring his father’s living with harlots, the father had killed the fatted calf for him.

The father said, “Son, you are always with me, and all that I have is yours. It was right that we should make merry and be glad, for your brother was dead and is alive again, and was lost and is found.”

scene.label: Ten silver coins
scene.text: Each coin was a drachma, a Greek silver coin worth about a day’s wage. For a poor woman, one coin in ten was a real loss. Village houses had few windows and floors of packed earth, so she needed a lamp and a broom to find it.

scene.label: His share
scene.text: With two sons, the younger would inherit a third, since the firstborn received a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17). Asking for it while his father still lived would probably have shamed the father deeply. Luke says the father divided his livelihood between them, so the older son’s share was settled too.

scene.label: Pigs and pods
scene.text: Pigs were unclean under the Law (Leviticus 11:7), so tending them for a Gentile was as low as a Jewish young man could fall. The pods were probably carob pods, used as animal feed and eaten only by the very poor.

scene.label: The father ran
scene.text: An older man of standing probably did not run in public in that culture; he would have had to gather up his long robes to do it. The father ran anyway, and he embraced his son before the young man had said a word.

scene.label: Robe, ring and sandals
scene.text: The best robe honored the son in front of everyone, a ring could carry the family’s authority, and sandals marked a son rather than a barefoot servant. A fatted calf was enough meat for a large crowd, so the celebration probably took in much of the village.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke records all three parables together; Matthew gives the lost sheep in another setting, as a warning not to despise the little ones (Matthew 18:12–14). Luke frames them with the grumbling about sinners and lets them build, from one sheep in a hundred to one coin in ten to one son of two. Luke, who loves to record joy, lets every parable end in a celebration.

seeing.reveals: Jesus explains His own table. He receives sinners because God goes looking for the lost and throws a feast when one comes home, and He invites even His critics to come in and share the joy.
seeing.living: Both sons were lost, one in a far country and one in the field next to the house. If you have wandered, come home; the Father is already watching the road. If you have stayed, ask whether you serve Him like a slave counting years, and go in to the feast when He welcomes someone you think does not deserve it.
seeing.ponder: Which son are you more like today, and what keeps you from going in to the Father’s feast?

preaching.big_idea: Heaven celebrates when the lost come home; the question is whether we will join the feast.
outline: The searching shepherd and the sweeping woman (3–10)
The younger son and the running father (11–24)
The older son and the pleading father (25–32)
preaching.watch_for: The father says “this my son” (v. 24). The older son says “this son of yours” (v. 30). The father replies, “your brother” (v. 32). The older son will not call him brother, and the father will not let him forget it.
